title: SLO-backed cost and latency claims catalog
content:
Purpose:
This working catalog is a pragmatic, sales-facing set of performance and unit-economics claims that are explicitly tied to SLOs and observable proof buckets. The goal: give AE/SE teams a safe set of language + evidence to use in discovery and demos, and a short validation plan to convert claims to contractual SLAs for Dedicated/Private deals.

Executive summary (one paragraph):
Buyers care about two things: consistent latency and predictable cost per user/session. Instead of aspirational performance numbers, we will present SLO-backed claims (e.g., "p95 inference time for 32-token replies on Dedicated <= 220ms under configured load") and an evidence matrix (benchmarks + production telemetry + customer pilots). That framing reduces negotiation friction and gives engineering buyers a clear path to verify in their environment.

Claim framework (how to write a claim):
- SLO anchor: choose a clear SLO and quantile (p50/p95/p99) + payload shape (tokens, concurrency).
- Deployment scope: hosted | dedicated | private; region and hardware profile.
- Model variant: model name + quantization/precision and any speed-optimized variant.
- Cost metric: per-1000 token cost, or per-session amortized CPU/GPU minutes at steady-state.
- Evidence type: lab benchmark, internal production telemetry, customer pilot, or independent benchmark.
- Fallback behavior: what happens on degradation (auto-failover to cheaper model or region).

Example candidate claims (draft wording for field use):
- "For Dedicated pools on A100-class hardware, Redwood observes p95 completion latency <= 260ms for typical 32-token assistant responses with batching optimized for 8 concurrent streams (internal lab benchmark, stable load)."
- "Hosted API default: median (p50) end-to-end generation time for 16-token responses < 120ms for curated small models; p95 varies by model and region—see evidence matrix."
- "End-to-end per-session cost can be reduced by up to 3.4x via prefix caching + model routing compared to a single-model baseline (measured in replayed enterprise chat workload)."

Evidence catalog (organize by evidence type):
- Lab benchmarks: tightly controlled runs using replayed traffic (ticket: JIRA-9876), accompanying scripts available in GH repo. Include: hardware spec, batch config, quantization, sequence lengths, request distribution.
- Production telemetry: anonymized, aggregated p95/p99 across customer clusters (safe-to-share bins: <250ms, 250-500ms, 500-1000ms).
- Customer pilots: short pilot templates (2–4 weeks) with clear instrumentation and expected convergence metrics.
- Independent benchmarks: third-party bench runs we can link to once available.

Proof point slices (high-value to sales):
1) Low-latency interactive assistants: p95 <= 300ms for short replies (<= 32 tokens) on Dedicated - evidence: lab + 2 pilot customers.
2) Cost per 1k tokens: show baseline (naive single-model) vs production config (batching, quant, cache) with delta and percent saving. Use a "dollars-per-1k-token" number for simplicity when talking to finance.
3) Tail stability under burst: show "90% of bursts resolve without AI-quality-impact fallback" and describe fallback policy.
4) Multi-tenant throughput: tokens/sec per GPU at steady-state and amortized cost per session for concurrent conversational workloads.

Competitive notes (short, for SE talking points):
- LargeCloudBox: claims high peak throughput but no transparent per-route SLOs or routing policies; customers often need to overprovision to hit p95 targets.
- ModelHub managed endpoints: flexible model catalog but limited prefix caching and batching; shows higher per-token cost on conversational workloads we replayed.
- OpenRuntime vendors: good raw performance on single-model runs; harder to operate at scale with multi-model routing and cross-region fallbacks.

Objections + concise rebuttals for field:
- "Your numbers are lab-only" -> "Agree; we always attach a pilot template and production telemetry bins. We include a three-stage verification path: lab benchmark, controlled pilot, ingest into your telemetry for final SLA."
- "How do you price for bursts?" -> "We show amortized per-session cost at steady-state and a burst-smoothing plan (reserve + burst pool) that protects latency SLOs while capping overage exposure."
- "What about hallucinations when using cheaper model fallbacks?" -> "Fallback policies are tied to quality gates and automatic rollback; pilots include prompt-preserving quality checks and automatic re-route to higher-fidelity variants if metric drift is detected."

Validation & go/no-go for formal marketing claims:
- Tier A claims (shareable externally): supported by lab + >=1 customer pilot + safety review.
- Tier B claims (partner/AE-only): lab + internal production telemetry.
- Tier C (internal): early lab runs, experimental configs.

Quick-play scripts for AE/SE (copy-paste friendly):
- Discovery opener: "What latency percentile and typical reply length are your users most sensitive to? Our SLO-first approach lets us map that directly to deployment options and estimated per-session costs."
- Pilot proposal blurb: "Two-week pilot: we'll deploy a Dedicated test pool, run your replay traffic, provide p50/p95/p99 reports, and a cost delta model comparing naive vs optimized configs."

Measurement artifacts to attach to proposals:
- replay-config.json (replay distribution used)
- bench-results.csv (p50/p95/p99 across seeds)
- cost-model.xlsx (amortized GPU minutes, tokens/second, $/1k tokens scenarios)

Open questions / forks to resolve (owner):
- Define safe public ranges for p95 claim buckets across our curated model catalog (owner: Priya Desai).
- Decide default pilot scope (2 vs 4 weeks) and acceptance criteria (owner: Liam O'Neill).
- Standardize cost-model workbook and assumptions for sales (owner: Marco Alvarez).

Next steps (this doc):
- Rapid review with SEs (1 week): gather favorite claim phrasings and missing evidence.
- Lock Tier A set (2 weeks): require pilots to complete and legal/marketing signoff.
- Build a one-pager "SLO-backed claims cheat sheet" and add to GTM toolkit.

Notes to self (draft-y):
- Keep language explicit: tie every numeric claim to a quantile, workload shape, and deployment. Avoid absolute superlatives like "fastest" unless we have apples-to-apples published bench.
- Wherever possible use relative deltas ("3x cheaper under X workload") with clear baseline definition.

---
End of draft.
summary: Working catalog for SLO-tethered latency and cost claims plus evidence catalog, pilot templates, competitive callouts and field scripts. Draft for SE/AE review.
